specPoints.text: understand how the current in a series circuit depends on the applied voltage and the number and nature of other components
understand why current is conserved at a junction in a circuit

primer.text: Wire two lamps one after another and they share a single loop; wire them side by side and the current gains choices. This note follows the current through both arrangements — unchanging along a series loop, splitting and recombining at the junctions of a parallel network — with charge conservation as the bookkeeping rule behind it all.

lessons.title: Current in series circuits
sourceHeadings: Increasing the voltage and number of components in series
lessons.opening: A series loop gives electrons exactly one road, so wherever you station a meter along it, the reading never changes. What does change the reading is the supply voltage and how many components share the loop. This lesson works both dials and reads the effect on the current.
keyPoints: A series circuit offers a single loop, so electrons have only one path to follow.
The current is the same at every point of a series loop.
A larger supply voltage drives a larger current around a series circuit.
Adding components in series raises the total resistance and so lowers the current.
The current size depends on both the source voltage and the number and type of components.

low.restatement: One loop, one current: every component in series carries exactly the same flow.
low.analogy: A single-lane ring road — every car that passes one tollbooth must pass them all, so the counts match.
low.examPointer: Quote 'same current at every point' when a question asks what an ammeter reads anywhere in a series loop.

medium.restatement: The loop's current is set by a tug-of-war: the supply voltage pushes harder, each extra component drags harder.
medium.analogy: Pedal harder (more voltage) and the bike speeds up; add more hills (more components) and it slows again.
medium.examPointer: Compare before-and-after circuits carefully: which knob moved, the voltage or the component count, decides which way the current goes.

check.stem: In a series circuit, the current at any point:

options.text: is the same everywhere in the loop
options.explanation: One path means the flow is identical at all points.

options.text: halves at each component it passes
options.explanation: Nothing consumes the current; it is not used up by components.
Position around the loop does not change a series current.

options.text: depends on where the ammeter sits
options.explanation: Every ammeter in the loop reads the same value.

check.stem: Increasing the voltage of the power source in a series circuit:

options.explanation: The voltage is one of the two dials that set the current.
A stronger push moves more charge, not less.

options.text: drives more current around the loop
options.explanation: A larger supply voltage drives a larger series current.
Resistance belongs to the components; the supply voltage does not change it.

check.stem: Adding more components to a series circuit:

options.text: raises total resistance and lowers the current
options.explanation: More series components add more opposition, so the flow drops.

options.text: raises total resistance and raises the current
options.explanation: The extra resistance chokes the flow instead of boosting it.
Series resistances add; they never shrink the total.

options.text: has no effect on the current
options.explanation: The component count is exactly what throttles a series current.

check.stem: A series circuit contains one cell and two identical lamps. If a third identical lamp is added in series, the current:

options.explanation: The extra lamp adds resistance, so the flow must drop.
More components in series means less current, not more.

options.text: drops because the loop's total resistance has grown
options.explanation: Three lamps oppose the charge more than two, so the loop carries a smaller current.
The direction of flow is set by the cell, not the lamp count.

options.text: get used up by the first component
options.explanation: Charge is never consumed; electrons keep circulating.

options.text: follow a single path through every component
options.explanation: A series loop offers one road and every electron takes it.
There are no branches in a series loop to choose between.
Charge cannot accumulate; what flows in must flow out.

check.stem: State two factors that set the size of the current in a series circuit.
check.modelAnswer: The voltage of the power source and the number and type of the other components, which fix the total resistance.

check.stem: What can you say about the current reading at different points of a series loop?
check.modelAnswer: Every ammeter in the loop reads the same value, because there is only one path for the charge.

check.stem: Explain why adding components in series reduces the current even though the voltage is unchanged.
check.modelAnswer: Each extra component adds its own resistance, so the loop's total resistance grows; with the supply voltage fixed, a larger resistance drives a smaller current.

check.stem: A series circuit has a 6 V cell and a total resistance of 12 Ω. Calculate the current, then predict the new current if the total resistance doubles to 24 Ω.
check.modelAnswer: I = V ÷ R = 6 V ÷ 12 Ω = 0.5 A. Doubling the total resistance to 24 Ω halves the current to 0.25 A.

lessons.title: Current in parallel circuits
sourceHeadings: Why is current conserved at a junction in a circuit?
lessons.opening: Give the electrons a choice of roads and the flow divides: some take one branch, some take another, and everyone rejoins further on. The rule that keeps it all honest is simple — whatever arrives at a junction must leave it. This lesson counts the currents at a junction and explains why the books always balance.
keyPoints: A parallel circuit gives electrons two or more loops to travel around.
Junctions are meeting points where the current splits into branches.
The branch currents add back up to the total current entering (and leaving) the junction.
Current is conserved at a junction because charge cannot be created or destroyed.
Branch currents share unequally unless the branches carry identical resistances.

low.restatement: At a junction the current splits among the branches, and the pieces always add back to the original.
low.analogy: A river forking around an island: the two channels together carry exactly what the main stream brought.
low.examPointer: Use the in-equals-out rule at each junction; label every branch current before doing any arithmetic.

medium.restatement: Conservation is exact bookkeeping: charge cannot pile up or vanish at a junction, so inflow equals outflow by necessity.
medium.analogy: A roundabout with equal entry and exit counts — cars neither materialise nor evaporate between junctions.
medium.examPointer: Branches split the current equally only when their resistances match; otherwise expect unequal shares.

check.stem: At a junction in a parallel circuit, the current:

options.explanation: Equal splitting needs identical branch resistances; otherwise shares differ.

options.text: is conserved: what flows in equals what flows out
options.explanation: Charge conservation makes the inflow and outflow match exactly.
Charge never vanishes; every arriving electron leaves along a branch.

options.text: doubles as it enters the branches
options.explanation: The branch currents sum back to the original, never beyond it.

check.stem: The current in each branch of a parallel circuit is equal only when:

options.explanation: Matching resistances share the current equally.
Length alone does not equalise the currents.

options.text: the supply voltage is very large
options.explanation: Voltage size cannot force equal branch currents.
The branch count is irrelevant to whether the shares match.

check.stem: A junction admits 10 A and one branch carries 6 A. The other branch carries:

options.explanation: Branches add to the total, so none can exceed it here.
Multiplying the two currents is meaningless.
10 − 6 = 4 A must flow in the remaining branch.
The 6 A branch already accounts for part of the total.

check.stem: Current is conserved at a junction because:

options.text: charge cannot be created or destroyed
options.explanation: The arriving charge has nowhere to go but out along the branches.

options.text: voltage cannot change at a junction
options.explanation: Voltage is the wrong quantity for this rule; the conservation is of charge.

options.text: resistance is zero at a junction
options.explanation: The rule holds whatever the resistances around it.
Repulsion is not the bookkeeping rule; charge conservation is.

check.stem: In a parallel circuit, the current at different points around the circuit:

options.text: is identical everywhere, as in a series loop
options.explanation: Parallel branches split the flow, so readings differ by position.

options.text: takes different values in different branches but the branch sums match the total
options.explanation: Branch currents differ, but they always add back to the junction total.
The branches each carry part of the total current.
Every branch carries the current in the same net direction around the loop.

check.stem: Define a junction and a branch in a parallel circuit.
check.modelAnswer: A junction is a point where two or more wires meet so the current can split; a branch is the stretch of circuit between two junctions.

check.stem: State the rule for the currents at a circuit junction.
check.modelAnswer: The total current flowing into the junction equals the total current flowing out along the branches.

check.stem: Explain why current is conserved at a junction.
check.modelAnswer: Current is the flow of charge, and charge cannot be created or destroyed; electrons reaching a junction must therefore leave along the branches, so the sums balance.

check.stem: A parallel circuit draws 9 A from the battery. One branch carries 4 A and a second carries 3 A. Find the third branch's current.
check.modelAnswer: The branches must total 9 A, so the third branch carries 9 − 4 − 3 = 2 A.

glossary.definition: A circuit with a single loop, so the same current passes through every component.
A circuit with two or more loops, letting the current split between branches.
A meeting point of wires where the current divides among branches.
A stretch of circuit lying between two junctions, carrying its own share of the current.
The principle that charge is neither created nor destroyed, so junction inflow equals outflow.
The drift of negative electrons through the wires, running opposite to conventional current.

workedExample.prompt: Ammeter A0 reads 10 A where the current leaves the battery; ammeter A1 sits in one branch and reads 6 A. Find the reading on ammeter A2 in the other branch.
steps: At the junction the current splits but is conserved, so the branch currents must add back to the total.
One branch takes 6 A, so the remaining branch carries 10 − 6.
